newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Egyptian envoy sees Israel's Netanyahu in peace bid.
newsitem.headline: Egyptian envoy sees Israel's Netanyahu in peace bid.

text.p: An Egyptian envoy met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday in a bid to revive Middle East peacemaking against the backdrop of clashes between Israeli soldiers and Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.

Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak's adviser, Osama el-Baz, went into a meeting with Netanyahu a few hours after Israeli troops shot and wounded two Palestinians during a confrontation with hundreds of protesters in Gaza.

"They fired live ammunition in the air and teargas and rubber bullets at the crowd," one witness told Reuters of the clash that erupted after Arabs knocked down a fence erected by Jewish settlers on property claimed by Palestinians.
El-Baz, who met Netanyahu for about two hours at a Tel Aviv hotel, planned to hold talks later with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in the West Bank self-rule enclave of Ramallah.

The Egyptian envoy hoped to arrange another round of deliberations between Israeli and Palestinian negotiators on reviving full-fledged peace talks suspended since Israel began building a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March.

"We believe that matters are moving in the right direction and we hope that developments will continue to move in that direction," he told reporters at the start of his meeting with the Israeli leader.
"The most important thing is to find a formula that will be acceptable to both parties for maintaining peace and stability and tranquility in the region."
Israel has said the Egyptian mediation was producing some progress but Palestinians said they did not expect a breakthrough and accused Israel of bargaining in bad faith.
"We appreciate the Egyptian role but at the same time we have no illusions," said Ahmed Abdel-Rahman, general secretary of Arafat's Palestinian Authority cabinet.

"Netanyahu is carrying out a game of public relations that aims to show false flexibility with the Egyptian initiative," he told Reuters, referring to reports Israel might freeze Jewish settlement construction in Jerusalem and the rest of the West Bank, the main bone of contention between Israel and the PLO.
Netanyahu has denied the reports, vowing to press ahead with the large housing project at the East Jerusalem site Israel calls Har Homa and Palestinians refer to as Jabal Abu Ghneim.

Egyptian mediation efforts, launched last month after U.S. envoy Dennis Ross failed to revive peacemaking, led this week to the first talks between Palestinian and Israeli negotiators since the deadlock.
"It is unlikely that a three-way meeting will take place before the weekend," said a senior Israeli official, who did not want to be identified.
Palestinians refuse to return to substantive negotiations until Israel halts settlement activities in the West Bank and and Gaza Strip.

Netanyahu, who after taking office a year ago lifted a partial freeze on Jewish settlement imposed by the prior dovish government he ousted in elections, says the construction does not violate peace deals.

El-Baz and Israeli officials said at the end of Sunday's talks that some progress had been made but Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat insisted the meeting did not mean the sides had resumed negotiations.
Israel occupied East Jerusalem in 1967 and claimed the whole city as its capital in a move not recognised internationally. Palestinians want East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state.
